subsection: 1. Change, resistance to change and fostering innovation

notes.b: Organisations (businesses, public bodies and not-for-profits) face change throughout their lives. It comes either from inside the business, where managers choose it, or from its environment, where they can only respond.
points: Internal changes are changes the organisation chooses or starts itself: new leadership, restructuring, the introduction of new technology, growth and the launch of new products.
A new chief executive can alter strategy, culture and priorities across the whole organisation, so the change reaches every department.
Restructuring reshapes reporting lines, roles and team structures, which changes who makes decisions and how work is shared.

External changes arise outside the firm, in the environment it cannot control. The STEEPLE factors (social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical) give a checklist for spotting them, and they assess external factors only.

External pressures include economic conditions, competitor actions, new regulation, technological developments, climate change and pandemics. The COVID-19 pandemic from March 2020 closed many workplaces and pushed firms towards remote working and online selling.

The key distinction is control: a business starts internal change and can only respond to external change. For a small business, hiring a new manager is internal, while a new competitor opening nearby is external.

New technology can be either. It is internal when the firm chooses to install it, such as moving to cloud systems or automation, and external when it arrives in the market and forces the firm to respond.
Digital technology can change how businesses operate and how consumers deal with them, an effect called disruptive impact, which can be positive and negative.

Climate change and environmental regulation are external pressures that push firms to cut waste and emissions. Ethical expectations from customers and staff, such as fair treatment and responsible sourcing, are also an external pressure to change.
notes.tip: When asked to identify or distinguish internal and external change, say which type each example is and why. A new competitor, a new law and a pandemic are external; a new manager, a restructuring and a new product launch are internal because the firm chooses them.

notes.b: Resistance to change is opposition, open or hidden, from people in an organisation to a planned change in how work is done. It is a natural human response, and managers need to understand its causes before they can address it.
points: Fear of job loss makes employees resist changes that may reduce headcount, change roles or cut hours. The effect is that staff may slow the change down or work against it to protect their positions.

Loss of status or control occurs when people believe they will lose influence, expertise or authority over their own work. A long-serving employee whose skills are made less valuable by a new system may therefore oppose it.
Uncertainty about what a change means for them leads people to resist it, even where the change is ultimately beneficial. People tend to prefer a known situation to an unknown one.
Habit makes people attached to familiar routines and reluctant to learn new methods or systems, so they keep using the old way and the change is adopted slowly.
Lack of trust in management, or lack of information about why the change is happening, fuels suspicion and opposition because staff fill the gap with the worst assumptions.
Extra workload during a transition, such as learning new software while keeping up with existing tasks, creates resistance because staff feel stretched and see the change as more work.
Resistance can also flag real problems with a plan, so managers should listen to the reasons behind it rather than simply override it.

Example (sample business): a family-run hotel replaces its paper booking diary with a cloud-based reservation system. Reception staff fear job loss, a long-serving receptionist feels she is losing status, and others are held back by habit and uncertainty about the busy season.
notes.tip: For an analyse question, give four distinct reasons and for each state the cause and its effect on the change or the business, tied to the business in the question. Common mistakes are naming reasons without explaining them, listing ways to overcome resistance instead of reasons, and giving two reasons that are really the same, such as uncertainty and lack of information.

notes.b: Resistance that is not handled can delay or derail change, so it has real costs for the organisation.
points: Resistance can slow implementation, so the benefits a change was meant to deliver arrive later than planned.
Staff who resist may reduce their productivity, lower the quality of their work or leave, which increases recruitment and training costs.
Widespread opposition can cause a change to fail completely, wasting the money and time already invested in it.
Handling change fairly and openly respects employees and sustains the trust that makes future change easier to achieve.
notes.tip: Always link back to the business in the question rather than describing these costs in general.

notes.b: Innovation is the creation and successful application of new ideas, products, processes or methods that add value for the organisation. An idea with no application is not innovation. It thrives where employees are encouraged to generate ideas and where failure is treated as a source of learning.
points: Empowerment gives employees the authority, information and resources to make decisions about their own work, so they can act on ideas without waiting for approval at every step.
Idea schemes give staff a formal route for submitting suggestions, which can then be assessed and rewarded. Online suggestion systems make this easy to run.

Time for projects lets staff work on new ideas during working hours rather than only in their spare time. For example, a software firm might give staff a fixed weekly time slot for their own projects.
Rewarding risk-taking signals that well-judged attempts are valued even when they do not succeed, which encourages staff to try new things.
Cross-functional teams bring together people from different departments, combining their skills and perspectives on a problem so ideas are tested from several angles.
Tolerance of failure allows experiments to be run and lessons learned without punishing the people involved, so staff are not afraid to suggest ideas.
Digital tools such as collaboration platforms and data used to test ideas can support idea generation. Innovation that cuts waste or energy use also supports sustainability.
Risk-taking must stay within legal and ethical limits, so encouraging staff to try new ideas does not mean accepting breaches of the law or unfair treatment of others.
notes.tip: To explain how a business can foster innovation, give three or four practices and the effect of each. Do not confuse innovation (new ideas applied successfully) with invention (a new idea).

notes.b: Both forms of thinking involve spotting opportunities and acting on them, but they differ in where the activity takes place and who carries the risk.
points: Entrepreneurial thinking means identifying an opportunity and accepting the financial risk of starting or growing a business to exploit it. The entrepreneur starts or runs the venture and bears its financial risk.
Intrapreneurial thinking (intrapreneurship) is entrepreneurial behaviour by an employee inside an existing organisation, such as developing a new product line for the employer.
An intrapreneur can deliver innovation for the employer without carrying the personal financial risk of founding a new business, which is the key difference from an entrepreneur.
Entrepreneurial thinking helps established firms adapt faster than competitors that rely only on existing routines, because staff keep looking for new ways to respond to change.
Business and financial literacy supports both forms of thinking, because an idea needs costing and a sound financial case before it can be pursued.
notes.tip: Both spot opportunities; only the entrepreneur founds the venture and bears the personal financial risk. Make that distinction explicit when asked to explain the difference.

notes.b: Managers can reduce resistance by addressing its cause, so the approach chosen should match the reason for opposition. Each reason is a cause; each approach below is an action by management.
points: Communication explains the reasons for the change, what it involves and how it affects each group. It reduces uncertainty and lack of information, and builds trust.
Consultation and participation involve employees in planning the change, which increases their sense of ownership of it and reduces loss of control.
Training builds the skills people need to work in the new way, addressing fear of failing or being left behind, and the pull of habit.
Support, such as coaching or extra help during the transition, eases the extra workload that change creates.
Negotiation and incentives offer something in return for accepting change, such as a bonus or an agreed guarantee about job security. This answers fear of job loss directly.
Leading by example shows that managers are personally committed to the change, which makes it more credible to staff and helps where trust is low.

Phased change introduces the change in stages. Its advantages are that people have time to adapt and managers can correct problems early. Its disadvantages are that it takes longer, prolongs uncertainty and gives opposition time to build up between stages.

Example (sample business): the family-run hotel gives early reassurance, involves staff in choosing and setting up the system, runs a trial period and provides hands-on training. For a return-to-office mandate, a firm can explain the reasons, consult staff and phase the change in.
notes.tip: For an outline question, name two approaches and state briefly how each reduces the resistance in the business in the question. Common mistakes are naming only one, stating an approach with no link to the business, and writing a long discussion where a short point per approach is needed.

keyTerms.definition: A change that originates inside the organisation, such as new leadership, restructuring, new technology, growth or new products.
A change that originates in the business environment outside the organisation, such as economic conditions, competitor action, regulation or climate.
Opposition, open or hidden, from people in an organisation to a planned change in how work is done.
The creation and successful application of new ideas, products, processes or methods that add value for the organisation.
Entrepreneurial behaviour by employees inside an existing organisation, who develop new ideas for their employer.
Giving employees the authority, information and resources to make decisions about their own work.
Introducing a change in stages over time rather than all at once.
A group drawn from different departments that works together on a shared task or project.

questions.prompt: A family-run Irish hotel plans to replace its paper booking diary with a cloud-based reservation system. Explain four reasons its staff might resist this change, and suggest how management could respond to each.
questions.model: Fear of job loss: staff may believe the system will reduce the number of reception and booking roles, so they resist it. Management could confirm early whether any roles will change, give written reassurance, and offer redeployment to guest services where possible. Loss of control and status: the receptionist who has run the paper diary for years may feel that her expertise is no longer valued. Management could involve these staff in choosing and configuring the system, so their knowledge shapes the change. Habit and uncertainty: experienced staff are comfortable with the diary and unsure how the new system will cope in the busy season, so they may keep using paper. Management could run a short trial period, provide hands-on training and set out clear guidance for the transition. Extra workload: learning the new system while the hotel is busy adds pressure, so a phased introduction, extra support in the first weeks and protected training time would ease the strain.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between internal and external sources of change, giving one example of each for a small retail business.
questions.model: An internal change starts inside the business and is usually controlled by its managers. For example, a shop owner who restructures the shifts or appoints a new store manager is making an internal change. An external change starts outside the business and is usually harder to control. For example, a new regulation on food labelling, or a rise in customer demand for locally sourced products, forces the shop to change its stock and displays.

questions.prompt: Explain how a business can foster innovation among its employees.
questions.model: A business can create an idea scheme that gives staff a formal route to submit suggestions, and it can reward good ideas with recognition or payment so that the scheme is taken seriously. It can also give employees time for projects during the working week, because innovation is unlikely to flourish if staff can only work on new ideas in their spare time. Cross-functional teams that combine people from sales, production and finance bring different perspectives to a problem and make creative solutions more likely. Finally, the business must tolerate failure, because employees will not experiment if they expect punishment for an unsuccessful attempt.
